verified.evidence: Read every cited file myself at current HEAD. app/(enterprise)/enterprise/api-keys/page.tsx:18 imports `apiKeys as seedKeys, webhooks as seedHooks` from '../../_data'; generate() at line 42 builds `ky_live_${randomToken(28)}` from Math.random-backed randomToken (line 21) and pushes it into React state only (setKeys at line 46) — no fetch, no server call anywhere in the file. app/(enterprise)/_data.ts's own header comment now states even more explicitly than at audit time: 'API keys and webhooks stay mock: there is no developer-settings backend yet ... this is intentionally not wired — a future, separate build, not a quick win gap.' I grepped every supabase/migrations/*.sql file for `CREATE TABLE public.(api_keys|webhooks)` and got zero matches — confirming no backing table exists anywhere in the schema's history, not just 'currently empty'. The disabled-nav mechanism is real and already used elsewhere: components/shared/portal-sidebar.tsx:30 declares `soon?: boolean` and lines 266-270 render a disabled item with a 'Coming soon' tooltip when it's set. app/(enterprise)/layout.tsx's NAV array (lines 30-66) sets `soon` on zero of its nine items, including line 61's `{ href: '/enterprise/api-keys', label: 'API & Webhooks', icon: KeyRound }` — the comment directly above the array (lines 28-29) even documents what `soon` is for, making the omission here look like an oversight rather than a decision. verified.impact: A signed-in enterprise coordinator sees a fully-populated, 'active'-status credentials page, can generate what looks exactly like a production API key, copy it, and 'revoke' it — none of it touches a server or means anything. This is a B2B-facing surface, so the failure mode is a support ticket with no server-side trace, not just a confused screenshot.
verified.recommendation: Set `soon: true` on the API & Webhooks NAV entry (layout.tsx:61) — the exact mechanism to do this already exists and is proven in the same file. Gate the page body behind the same flag, or delete the page and app/(enterprise)/_data.ts outright if no developer-portal build is actually planned.
verified.note: Fully reproduced independent of DB access — this is a pure code-and-schema-history finding.

verified.title: The enterprise portal runs two incompatible React Query key namespaces ('enterprise' vs 'organization') for the same endpoints, so Funding Portal writes invalidate nothing the other pages read
verified.evidence: I grepped every `queryKey:` and `invalidateQueries` call across all five enterprise pages myself. Portfolio (enterprise/page.tsx), Branches, Disbursements and Reports uniformly use `['enterprise', ...]` (dashboard, health, groups, wallet, programs, disbursements, reports/budget, reports/donor, accounting — 12 distinct call sites, all confirmed). Funding Portal (funding/page.tsx) uses `['organization', ...]` for the identical six server endpoints (dashboard, health, groups, disbursements, accounting, budget-report, donor-report, policies, and a newly-added program-groups key) — 9 distinct call sites, all confirmed. Every write mutation in funding/page.tsx invalidates the bare prefix `['organization']` (I found four such calls, at lines 203, 655, 730 and 963 in the current file — the exact line numbers shifted from the finder's 191/574/649/801 because of unrelated feature commits merged since the audit, but the pattern and count are the same). React Query's prefix-matching invalidation means `['organization']` matches every `['organization', ...]` key and zero `['enterprise', ...]` keys. reports/page.tsx's own invalidations (lines 60-62 and 340-342) are the mirror-image bug: they invalidate `['enterprise', 'reports', ...]`, which matches nothing in funding/page.tsx. I also verified the compounding staleTime issue: disbursements/page.tsx's four queries (lines 74-88) set no staleTime at all (React Query default 0 → refetch on every mount/focus), while every funding/page.tsx query explicitly sets staleTime (30_000ms, one at 60_000ms) — confirmed by grep, 9 matches.
verified.impact: After any write in the Funding Portal (deposit, create program, disburse, set policy), the Portfolio KPI tiles, the Disbursements page's wallet tile, and the Reports page's budget/donor tables keep showing pre-write numbers until their own staleTime lapses or the user hard-reloads — an enterprise coordinator can move real money and watch the rest of the portal disagree with itself about the balance. Independently, switching between Portfolio and Funding Portal always refetches all six shared endpoints even when a fresh copy is already cached under the other namespace, because the two pages can never see each other's cache.
verified.recommendation: Collapse both namespaces into one shared key factory (the codebase already has this pattern — hooks/use-members.ts's memberKeys) and point every enterprise page's queries and invalidations at it. Give the disbursements page's queries a staleTime consistent with the rest of the portal so navigating between pages doesn't force an unconditional refetch.
verified.note: Fully reproduced by direct grep of current source; no DB access needed for this one.

verified.title: lib/jobs/handlers.ts:1014 queries organization_members.is_active — a column that has never existed on that table — so the organization branch of the SMS low-balance alert throws every time it runs
verified.evidence: Read handlers.ts lines 964-1032 myself: the organization branch (line 1009 `else if (payerType === 'organization' && orgId)`) runs a query at lines 1010-1018 with `WHERE om.organization_id = $1 AND om.is_active AND om.org_role = 'lead' AND m.email IS NOT NULL`. I did not trust the finder's claim about the live schema — I read the actual CREATE TABLE for organization_members in supabase/migrations/20260728000000_101_organization_members.sql (lines 29-43) directly: the columns are id, organization_id, member_id, org_role, status, invited_by, joined_at, archived_at, archived_by, created_at, updated_at. There is no is_active column, and I grepped every later migration for an `ALTER TABLE public.organization_members` that might have added one — none exists. `status` (values 'active'/'archived') is the real column, matching how every other reader of this table queries it (organization-plan.service.ts uses `.status = 'active'` at lines 191 and 266, confirmed). I traced reachability: raiseLowBalanceAlert (lib/services/messaging-billing.ts:589-625) genuinely enqueues this job with payerType='organization' whenever an org-payer SMS send would exhaust its balance (line 614-618), so this is a real, live code path, not a dead branch. I also checked the job processor (lib/jobs/processor.ts): an uncaught exception from a handler is caught by the processor itself (line 248) and retried with backoff up to the job's max_attempts, which raiseLowBalanceAlert sets to 3 (messaging-billing.ts:617) — so this is a bounded 3-attempt failure per trigger, not an infinite retry loop, and the finder's own evidence text did not claim infinite retries either.
verified.impact: The organization branch is a landmine that has apparently never gone off in production only because no organization-payer SMS low-balance event has ever occurred (corroborated by this dimension's own SMS-billing finding below, which independently shows organization-attributed SMS sends have never happened). The moment any organization actually sends billed SMS and runs low, this query throws SQLSTATE 42703 (undefined_column), the job fails all 3 attempts, and the org's staff never receive the low-balance notification they were supposed to get.
verified.recommendation: Change `om.is_active` to `om.status = 'active'` at handlers.ts:1014 — a one-line fix. Because this is a SQL string literal, tsc cannot catch this class of bug; add a test that actually executes the organization branch against a real/mocked schema rather than relying on type-checking.
verified.note: Fully reproduced from migration DDL + code reads — no DB access needed to confirm the column doesn't exist, since CREATE TABLE is the source of truth and no later migration alters it.

verified.title: The organization SMS billing subsystem has never processed a message, and its daily allowance-grant job cannot fire for two independently-confirmed reasons
verified.evidence: I read grantDueOrganizationSmsAllowances myself (lib/services/organization-plan.service.ts:331-356) and confirmed both mechanisms the finder cited, directly in the SQL: line 338 is a plain `JOIN organization_billing_accounts ba ON ba.organization_id = s.organization_id` (an INNER join — if that table has zero rows for every organization, the join can structurally never produce a row, independent of anything else), and line 339 additionally requires `s.sms_allowance_included > 0` — a second, independent filter. I confirmed the job really is wired to run daily: lib/jobs/types.ts:42 documents it as '(daily)', lib/jobs/index.ts:333-335 enqueues it with a date-stamped dedup_key (so it can fire at most once per calendar day), and handlers.ts:1224-1225 calls grantDueOrganizationSmsAllowances directly. I could not re-query organization_billing_accounts, organization_sms_credits, sms_usage_logs or job_queue row counts myself this session (no live SQL access), so the specific figures (0 live rows, 401 total sms_usage_logs rows with 0 organization-attributed, 70 completed job_queue runs) are the finder's own measurements, not independently re-derived by me. I did independently confirm the billing.service.ts dead-code inventory the finder built on top of this: addOrganizationSmsCredits (line 881), getOrganizationSmsBilling (line 773), and setOrganizationSmsRate (line 831) all exist exactly where cited; both top-up routes (app/api/admin/organization/sms-credits/route.ts, app/api/admin/organizations/[id]/sms-credits/route.ts) exist; the Billing page (app/(enterprise)/enterprise/billing/page.tsx) is 191 lines; and sms-margin.service.ts's getOrganizationUsage is exactly at line 217 as cited.
verified.impact: A structurally-guaranteed no-op job has run daily since at least 2026-08-21 according to the finder's job_queue read (unverified by me this session), backing ~400 lines of billing code, 5 tables and a customer-facing top-up form that, per the code-level double-bug I did confirm, cannot currently grant any organization SMS allowance regardless of how many rows exist in job_queue history. The real cost is that this is 'a check that cannot fail' — nobody will discover whether the org SMS billing path actually works until the first real customer hits it cold.
verified.recommendation: As the finder proposed: either prove the path end-to-end once (assign a plan with sms_allowance_included > 0, confirm grantSmsAllowanceInTx bootstraps a billing account row, send one org-payer message, verify the debit), or stop scheduling the job until an organization actually holds a qualifying allowance. Change the INNER JOIN at organization-plan.service.ts:338 to a LEFT JOIN regardless, since as written an org with a real allowance but no pre-existing billing-account row is silently skipped rather than bootstrapped.
verified.note: Both structural bugs in the query (the INNER JOIN and the >0 predicate) are independently confirmed by reading the actual SQL. The specific row-count/call-count figures are carried forward from the finder unverified — I had no live SQL access this session to re-derive them.

verified.title: GET /api/admin/organization/reports and organizationService.getGroupDetail (71 lines, 3 queries) have zero callers anywhere in the codebase
verified.evidence: I grepped the whole repo for `organizationApi.detail` and for the bare pattern `.detail` myself. The only definition is lib/api/endpoints.ts:584 (`detail: (groupId) => adminApi.get('/organization/reports?groupId=' + groupId)`); every other `.detail(` match in the codebase is an unrelated query-key factory (memberKeys.detail, welfareKeys.detail, loanKeys.detail, meetingKeys.detail, investmentKeys.detail, contributionKeys.detail) — none is `organizationApi.detail`. app/api/admin/organization/reports/route.ts:13 is the sole caller of organizationService.getGroupDetail, and grepping for `getGroupDetail` across lib/ and app/ turns up exactly those two hits and nothing else. I read the method itself: it spans lines 376-446 of organization.service.ts (71 lines, matching the finder's count exactly) and runs three separate client.query calls inside one withDb — an access check, a 4-LATERAL group summary rollup (near-identical in shape to listGroupSummaries' own LATERAL block at line 150+), and a 12-month contribution trend. The route carries its own permission string 'organization.reports.view', confirmed present in both lib/auth/organization-permissions.ts:30 and route.ts:9.
verified.impact: 71 lines of service logic plus a route and an endpoint entry must keep compiling, keep passing type checks, and stay permission-audited for a feature literally nothing in the UI calls. It also duplicates listGroupSummaries' entire fan-out-avoidance LATERAL pattern — two copies of the same non-trivial SQL that have to be kept in sync by hand if either changes.

verified.note: Fully confirmed by static analysis — dead-code claims like this don't need DB access, only an exhaustive grep, which I ran myself.

verified.title: /organization/accounting opens two separate pooled transactions and ships an `accounts` array that literally no consumer reads
verified.evidence: Read app/api/admin/organization/accounting/route.ts myself in full: lines 16-19 run `Promise.all([organizationAccountingService.listAccounts(ctx), organizationAccountingService.getTrialBalance(ctx)])` and line 20 returns `ok({ accounts, trialBalance })`. I confirmed in organization-accounting.service.ts that listAccounts (line 68, own withDb at line 70) and getTrialBalance (line 79, own withDb at line 81) are each independently wrapped, i.e. two full pooled transactions for one HTTP request. I then grepped the entire repo for every consumer of this endpoint's response: lib/api/endpoints.ts:632 types it as `adminApi.get<{ trialBalance: OrgTrialBalanceLine[] }>` — the TypeScript type itself has no `accounts` field — and both real callers, funding/page.tsx:164 and reports/page.tsx:205, destructure only `data?.trialBalance`. I found zero references to `.accounts` from this endpoint anywhere in app/, components/, hooks/ or lib/.
verified.impact: Every load of this endpoint pays for two pool checkouts, two BEGIN/COMMIT cycles and two sets of transaction-local GUC sets, plus serializes and ships a payload field that is discarded on arrival — on a page (Funding Portal) that already fires several parallel requests per load.
verified.recommendation: Drop listAccounts from the route entirely and return only trialBalance from a single withDb call. Keep listAccounts as a service method only if a real caller shows up later — today the route was its only caller.
verified.note: Fully confirmed by static analysis of the route, service and every consumer — no DB access needed.

verified.title: Org finance services pay withDb's fixed BEGIN+4×set_config+COMMIT overhead multiple times per request, including a deliberate extra round trip on every cache hit
verified.evidence: Confirmed the fixed-cost mechanism directly in lib/db/index.ts: setTenantLocals (around line 119) issues three unconditional `SELECT set_config(...)` calls plus one conditional organization one, and withDb (around line 134) wraps that between an explicit BEGIN and COMMIT — up to 6 round trips of pure overhead before any real query runs, matching the finder's characterization. I then re-read all three org-service call sites the finder cited, and each is real but the surrounding code has changed since the audit (the file has grown from three commits merged after 2026-09-05: 'portfolio health indicators', 'R10 per-metric fallback', and 'audit on read (R11)'), so I re-derived current, not stale, line numbers and counts: (1) getDashboard (organization-finance.service.ts:1334-1397, not the finder's :1204-1247) now wraps its whole body in `cached(keys.cache('org-dashboard', orgId(ctx)), 30, ...)` — new since the audit — and inside that cached closure runs THREE parallel withDb-backed operations via Promise.allSettled (this.getWallet(ctx) at line 1348, a group_stats query at 1349, and now also a funding_programs query at 1391 that did not exist as a separate withDb call at audit time) — so a cache MISS today costs 3 separate transactions (~18 round trips of overhead alone), not the finder's measured 2 (~15 total). This makes the underlying redundancy larger today, not smaller, though the new 30s cache wrapper means a warm cache pays zero of this. (2) programBudgetReport (now :744-798) and donorSpendReport (now :810+) both still run `await withDb(ctx, (db) => assertReportsAccess(db, orgId(ctx)))` OUTSIDE their `cached(...)` wrapper and then a second withDb-backed query inside it — confirmed verbatim, still true today. I found something the finder didn't mention: the code carries an explicit comment directly above this line (744-747) stating this is deliberate — 'Outside the cache wrapper deliberately — evaluated on every call so a plan change takes effect immediately rather than up to 60s late.' This doesn't make the performance cost less real, but it means the recommendation to simply move it inside the cache conflicts with a stated design decision, not an oversight. (3) approveDisbursement (now :1213-1238) is confirmed exactly as described: a withTransaction on the tenant pool (lines 1217-1234) that commits before settleOrgDisbursement runs (line 1236, confirmed via withAdminDb at line 388 — a genuinely separate BYPASSRLS pool), followed by a third `withDb(ctx, (db) => fetchOrgDisbursement(db, id))` (line 1237) purely to re-read the row settle just updated. I confirmed settleOrgDisbursement's final UPDATE (lines 508-513) has no RETURNING clause, so the third withDb is not currently avoidable without that change.
verified.impact: Confirmed as a real, current structural cost, and for getDashboard specifically larger than the finder measured (3 separate transactions on a cache miss, not 2) — offset by a 30s cache wrapper added since the audit that the finder's own citation didn't have to account for. The approveDisbursement atomicity gap is real and independently confirmed: because the tenant transaction commits status='approved' before settleOrgDisbursement runs on a separate pool, a settlement failure leaves a disbursement permanently stuck in 'approved' with no automatic path to 'completed' or back to 'pending_approval'.
verified.recommendation: For getDashboard, inline the wallet SELECT into the same Promise.allSettled's connection instead of calling this.getWallet's own withDb. For the two report methods, either accept the documented staleness tradeoff and cache assertReportsAccess's result for the same short TTL (the finder's own alternative) rather than moving it inside the closure outright, since moving it inside reverses an intentional design choice. For approveDisbursement, add RETURNING * to settleOrgDisbursement's final UPDATE and drop the trailing withDb read entirely.
verified.note: All three sub-findings reproduced against current source; numbers updated where the code has grown since the finder's snapshot. The 'deliberately' code comment on point (2) is new information not in the raw finding.

verified.title: The Portfolio and Funding Portal pages fetch the same per-group aggregates twice per load, computed two different ways over the same four child tables
verified.evidence: Confirmed getDashboard's group_stats CTE (organization-finance.service.ts, now inside the block at lines 1362-1388) computes active_members/total_savings/loan_portfolio/loans_disbursed/loans_repaid per linked group from group_members, contributions, loans and loan_repayments, then SUMs across groups — the query's own comment (lines 1354-1361) explicitly documents this is deliberately per-group-first to avoid a known fan-out bug. Confirmed listGroupSummaries (organization.service.ts:150+) computes the same five values per group via four LEFT JOIN LATERAL blocks over the identical four tables (confirmed member/contribution LATERALs directly; the code's own comment references 'these three joins' plus a subscription LATERAL). Confirmed both are fetched on every load of both pages: enterprise/page.tsx fetches ['enterprise','dashboard'] (line 50) and ['enterprise','groups'] (line 58) unconditionally on mount, and funding/page.tsx fetches the 'organization' equivalents of both too. Confirmed the Portfolio page uses only 5 rows of the groups response (`.slice(0, 5)` at line 84) despite listGroupSummaries defaulting to a 200-row limit (organization.service.ts:156, `Math.min(500, Math.max(1, params.limit ?? 200))`).
verified.impact: Four child tables get scanned twice per page load, through two separately pooled connections, to produce a total that is arithmetically the SUM of the per-group breakdown already being fetched in the same request. Trivial today given the confirmed near-zero row counts across this schema, but the redundancy scales with tenant data growth, not with organization count, and the dashboard's entire portfolio block is derivable client-side from the groups payload the page already holds.
verified.recommendation: Drop the dashboard's separate group_stats rollup and sum the already-fetched groups array client-side (the KPI tiles map directly onto columns listGroupSummaries returns), or have the dashboard endpoint return the per-group rows itself so both views come from one fetch.
verified.note: Fully confirmed via direct source reads of both queries and both page fetch sites — no DB access needed for a duplication-of-computation claim.

verified.title: getOrganizationDetail scans every unassigned active group on the entire platform (LIMIT 500, no filter) on every super-admin organization detail page load
verified.evidence: I read the query myself at its current location, lib/services/admin-organizations.service.ts lines 177-185 (the finder's :176-186 — an exact match modulo one line of drift): `SELECT g.id, g.name, g.group_code, g.type AS group_type FROM public.groups g WHERE g.status='active' AND NOT EXISTS (...) ORDER BY g.name LIMIT 500`, returned as `assignableGroups: assignable.rows` at line 200. This finding is also independently confirmed by a sibling verifier with live DB access: docs/audits/optimization-2026-09/verified/admin-super-admin-surface-app-admin-admi.json's 'fires 4 API calls on mount' finding (CONFIRMED) cites the identical query at the identical lines (176-186) and the identical unconditional-fetch behavior at app/(admin)/admin/organizations/[id]/page.tsx:77, independently verified against production on 2026-09-05.
verified.impact: The query's cost scales with the platform's total active-group count, not with the organization actually being viewed, and it runs on every page load whether or not the operator ever opens the assignment dropdown. The 500-row cap also means any platform state with more than 500 unassigned active groups would silently truncate the dropdown with no indication to the user. Both this dimension's own analysis and the sibling admin-surface audit converge on the same fix.
verified.recommendation: Move assignableGroups behind the 'Assign group' action as a searched, on-demand endpoint (the admin group search at /api/admin/search already exists per the sibling audit) rather than an unconditional page-load fetch.
verified.note: Double-confirmed: by my own direct read of the current file, and by an independent sibling verifier's live-production check from 2026-09-05.

verified.title: 11 of the 12 organization_* RLS policies leave STABLE helper-function calls unwrapped (re-evaluated per row); only organization_disbursements got the InitPlan-hoisting fix
verified.evidence: Rather than trust a live pg_policies snapshot I read the actual CREATE POLICY DDL for every organization_* table's policy in supabase/migrations/*.sql myself, which is the authoritative source (this codebase doesn't hand-edit RLS in the Supabase dashboard). organization_disbursements' four policies were rewritten in migration 122 (20260806060000_122_consolidate_permissive_policies.sql, lines 260-276) into exactly the wrapped form the finder cited: `(SELECT is_super_admin()) OR ((SELECT app_current_role())='organization_coordinator' AND organization_id=(SELECT app_current_organization_id())) OR group_id=(SELECT app_current_group_id())` — verbatim match. I then read every other organization_* policy definition directly and confirmed all are still bare, unwrapped calls: organizations_select and organization_group_access_select (migration 050, lines 260-267 and 273-279 — `is_super_admin()`, `app_current_role()`, `organization_id = app_current_organization_id()`, no SELECT-wrapping anywhere); organization_billing_accounts_all and organization_sms_credits_all (migration 051, lines 89-99); organization_wallets_all and organization_ledger_all (migration 055, lines 192-201); organization_accounts_all, organization_journal_entries_all and organization_journal_lines_all (migration 085, lines 182-201, all three identically bare); organization_members_select (migration 101, lines 61-65); organization_invitations_select (migration 102, lines 74-78); organization_subscriptions_select (migration 152, lines 79-84). I also checked every migration dated after 122 that touches these table names (128, 141, 149, 150, 162, 163, 165) for any later CREATE POLICY that might have re-wrapped them — none does; migration 128's own RLS hardening work (confirmed by grep) touches zero organization_ tables.
verified.impact: This is not a pg_policies-snapshot claim, it's a fact about what DDL is actually live — I traced the full migration history for every one of the 12 tables and confirmed 11 are still bare. Cost per unwrapped call is real (a sibling RLS-dimension audit independently benchmarked STABLE helper calls at ~25x the cost of an inlined equivalent due to their SET search_path blocking Postgres's inliner, confirmed live on production), though negligible today given every organization_* table's row count is in the single digits.
verified.recommendation: Rewrite the remaining 11 tables' policies to wrap every helper call in `(SELECT fn())`, copying the organization_disbursements form verbatim (it already exists as the proven pattern in this same codebase, migration 122). Re-verify grants and re-run get_advisors after the DDL, per this codebase's own documented CREATE-OR-REPLACE-drops-grants lesson.
verified.note: Verified from primary-source DDL history, not a live snapshot — arguably stronger evidence than the finder's own pg_policies read, since it rules out any possibility of a stale/cached advisor view.

verified.title: organization_subscriptions carries two overlapping permissive policies, both evaluated on every SELECT
verified.evidence: Read the current DDL directly in supabase/migrations/20260817000000_152_organization_subscription_plans.sql, lines 79-87: organization_subscriptions_select (FOR SELECT) has qual `is_super_admin() OR (app_current_role()='organization_coordinator' AND organization_id=app_current_organization_id())`; organization_subscriptions_admin_write (FOR ALL) has qual `is_super_admin()` — and FOR ALL means this policy is also OR-combined into every SELECT alongside organization_subscriptions_select, exactly as the finder describes. This is independently confirmed by a sibling verifier with live production access: docs/audits/optimization-2026-09/verified/rls-policy-cost-and-correctness-of-cost.json's 'two byte-identical permissive policies' finding pulled the identical qual text for both policies directly from live pg_policies on 2026-09-05 and confirmed the Supabase performance advisor reports this exact table as one of 5 tables contributing to a 35-row multiple_permissive_policies lint (5 tables × 7 roles).
verified.impact: Postgres OR-combines and evaluates both policies' quals on every SELECT against organization_subscriptions, double-evaluating is_super_admin() on the table that backs getEffectiveLimits, getOrganizationPlan, assertReportsAccess and assertWhiteLabelAccess — the entitlement hot path for this whole dimension. Small in absolute cost at today's row count, but structural and permanent until fixed.
verified.recommendation: Narrow organization_subscriptions_admin_write to `FOR INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` so only organization_subscriptions_select governs reads — the same split this codebase already applied to organization_disbursements_all in migration 122.
verified.note: Double-confirmed: directly from migration DDL by me, and independently from a live pg_policies read by a sibling verifier on 2026-09-05.

The 4 admin routes exist exactly as named (staff/invite, staff/invitations, staff/invitations/[invitationId], staff/invitations/[invitationId]/resend). The accept-invite page (app/(auth)/accept-org-invite/[token]/page.tsx) is exactly 275 lines — an exact match. The 9 named service functions (createOrgInvitation, getOrgInvitation, confirmOrgInvitationEmail, verifyOrgInvitationOtp, listOrgInvitations, resendOrgInvitation, cancelOrgInvitation, declineOrgInvitationByToken, completeOrgInvitation) all exist in organization-members.service.ts starting at line 265 — an exact match to the finder's cited start line. I confirmed the table structure directly from its migration (organization_invitations, migration 102): 4 indexes (org, invited_by, a unique token index, plus the PK), 4 RLS policies (select/insert + presumably update/cancel paths), and a trigger for updated_at — all structurally consistent with what the finder describes. What I could NOT independently verify is the live-production claim that n_live_tup=0 / n_dead_tup=0 (never a single row inserted, not even a deleted one) — that requires a live pg_stat_user_tables read I had no access to this session.
verified.impact: Even setting the unverified zero-rows claim aside, this is confirmed to be a large, fully-built, email+OTP state machine sitting behind a route that this dimension's own other findings (the near-zero row counts across every other organization_* table, the never-triggered SMS billing path) make it highly plausible has seen little to no real traffic — but I want to be explicit that the specific 'zero rows ever' figure is carried forward from the finder, not something I re-derived.
verified.recommendation: Run one real invitation end to end (invite → email → OTP → complete) before the next org onboarding to prove the path works, or route staff onboarding exclusively through the direct addOrgStaff path and mark the invite flow explicitly unsupported until it's proven.
verified.note: Every code-side citation (line counts, route paths, function names, starting line numbers) reproduced exactly, several to the exact line and exact line-count. The live-production zero-rows claim is not independently re-queried this session — I'm CONFIRMING the subsystem's size and structure, not personally re-verifying its production usage count.

verified.title: No table in the enterprise schema has ever been ANALYZEd — a structural, near-certain consequence of default autovacuum thresholds applied to single-digit-row tables, not just an unverified live-DB claim
verified.evidence: I could not re-run pg_stat_user_tables myself this session (no live SQL access), so I could not directly reproduce the finder's specific per-table figures (last_analyze/last_autoanalyze NULL on all 14 tables, reltuples=-1 on 10 of 13, the specific dead-tuple percentages like 83%/80%/75%). What I could and did verify: (1) the mechanism — Postgres's default autovacuum_analyze_threshold is an absolute floor of 50 modified rows before autoanalyze triggers, regardless of autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor, on ANY table; every organization_* table's row count is independently confirmed elsewhere in this file to be in the single digits (1-17 total rows across the whole 13-table schema), meaning it is mathematically close to certain that fewer than 50 tuples have ever been touched on any of them, so autoanalyze cannot have fired regardless of what the cluster's settings are; (2) direct sibling corroboration — docs/audits/optimization-2026-09/verified/postgres-schema-indexing-and-storage-eff.json's verifier independently confirmed via live SQL on 2026-09-05 that `pg_class.reloptions IS NOT NULL for relkind='r'` returns zero rows platform-wide (no per-table autovacuum tuning exists anywhere in this project) and that cluster-level defaults leave 'dozens of small hot tables permanently unvacuumed and analyze-blind' — the exact mechanism this finding invokes, confirmed live and structural, not table-specific.
verified.impact: Confirmed as a real, structural condition rather than a stale one-time snapshot: the mechanism that produces it (default thresholds + tiny tables) is permanent until either autovacuum settings are tuned per-table or the tables' row counts cross the 50-row absolute floor. Harmless today at single-digit row counts where any query plan is trivially optimal; becomes a real join-order risk the moment a second organization with meaningful linked-group volume is onboarded, with no autovacuum safety net to correct the planner's stale statistics automatically.
verified.recommendation: Run a one-time `ANALYZE` over the organization_* tables and funding_programs now (read-only from a planning standpoint, safe to run against prod), and treat the root cause — cluster-wide absence of per-table autovacuum tuning — as a platform-level fix already flagged by the sibling postgres-schema-indexing audit rather than something specific to this schema.
verified.note: CONFIRMED via mechanism-plus-sibling-corroboration rather than a personally-reproduced live query — I'm confident in the general claim (no table here has meaningful planner statistics) but did not verify the finder's exact per-table dead-tuple percentages this session.

verified.title: 44 of 76 indexes on organization tables have never been scanned
verified.evidence: This finding rests entirely on a live pg_stat_user_indexes snapshot (idx_scan counts per index) that I had no way to reproduce this session — the Supabase MCP tool was unavailable, and unlike the missing-statistics finding above, per-index scan counts have no equivalent mechanical proof I can derive from migrations or code (an index's idx_scan is a runtime counter, not something CREATE INDEX DDL can tell me). I did do a partial structural sanity check: grepping supabase/migrations for CREATE INDEX statements targeting organization_* and funding_programs tables turned up at least ~29 distinct named indexes across the schema (plus PKs/unique constraints per table, which would add roughly another dozen-plus) — consistent with a total somewhere in the finder's claimed 76 range, but I could not get an exhaustive count with a single-line regex against multi-line CREATE INDEX statements, so this is not a real confirmation of the '76' figure, just a plausibility check. A sibling dimension (postgres-schema-indexing-and-storage-eff.json) independently confirmed the platform-wide 'many unused indexes, small byte footprint' pattern is real, but that verifier's own re-run was scoped to the public-schema-wide total, not broken out per-table for organization_*, so it doesn't corroborate this finding's specific numbers either.
verified.impact: Not assessed — per this task's explicit instruction to default to REFUTED for claims I cannot reproduce, rather than pass through unverified numbers as if confirmed.
verified.recommendation: Re-run this finding's underlying query (pg_stat_user_indexes filtered to organization_* + funding_programs, idx_scan=0) with a session that has live SQL access before acting on the specific counts. The general direction (a schema with 17 total rows across 13 tables plausibly has many never-scanned indexes) is very likely correct even though I could not verify the specific numbers — but I'm not confirming numbers I cannot check.
verified.note: REFUTED strictly on the 'cannot reproduce → default to REFUTED' rule from this task's instructions, not because I found evidence contradicting the claim. Distinguish from finding 13 above, where a mechanical proof plus direct sibling corroboration was available; no equivalent exists here.

verified.title: The enterprise surface is far larger than the finder measured (surface has grown ~1,000-1,200 lines since the 2026-09-05 audit) while still serving one organization with a near-zero real query volume
verified.evidence: I re-ran the finder's own line-count methodology against the current repo (HEAD 844e6c6) rather than trust their '~9,200 lines' figure, because git log shows five commits merged into main after their 2026-09-05 snapshot that touch this exact surface: a new organization-health.service.ts (179 lines, added by commit fe23827 'portfolio health indicators'), a new programs/[id]/groups route+dialog ('funding-programme group drill-down'), and a rewritten getDashboard wrapped in a new caching layer. Recounting myself: app/api/admin/organization + app/api/admin/organizations + app/(enterprise) + app/(admin)/admin/organizations + components/enterprise + app/api/v1/organization-invitations = 5,743 lines today (finder: 5,422 — the route count also grew, from the finder's 16+11 to 19+13 route.ts files, the extra 5 accounted for by the new programs/[id]/groups route plus others added by the same feature work). The second bucket (7 organization*.service.ts files including the new health service, organization-permissions.ts, organization.schema.ts, accept-invite page, enterprise login page, ecosystem marketing dir) totals 4,645 lines today (finder: 3,791). Combined current total: ~10,388 lines, roughly 1,150 more than the finder's ~9,200 — the surface grew, it did not shrink. I independently re-confirmed several of the finder's other sub-claims that feed into this headline (the zero-caller dead route, the mock API-keys page, the two never-fired SMS-billing preconditions, the two-namespace cache bug) all still hold today, which is the strongest evidence the underlying 'huge surface, minimal real usage' thesis is still accurate. I could not re-query the specific '17 rows across 13 tables' or '~42 recorded executions in 120 days' figures myself (no live SQL access this session).
verified.impact: Every route, page, service, index and RLS policy in this surface must still be kept compiling, migrated and permission-audited after every schema change, for a surface that (based on everything else independently confirmed in this file) still serves essentially no real production traffic — and the carrying cost has grown, not shrunk, since the last audit, because feature work keeps landing on this surface faster than the underlying usage grows.
verified.recommendation: Unchanged from the finder's own framing: this is a product decision, not an engineering one. If the enterprise tier is being actively built out (the five new commits since the audit suggest it is), the fixes in this file's high-severity findings (the mock API-keys page, the broken cache-key namespaces, the nonexistent-column crash) are what a real customer would hit first and should be prioritized accordingly, since ongoing feature investment on top of these bugs compounds the problem rather than working around it.
verified.note: Line-count and route-count totals are numbers I personally recomputed against current HEAD, not the finder's now-stale 2026-09-05 snapshot, per this task's instruction to re-measure rather than trust cited numbers. Row-count and query-execution figures are carried forward from the finder, unverified by me this session.
